metadata.title: Why Wrapping the Same Text in XML Changes the Answer Claude Gives
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: why does wrapping the same text in XML change Claude's answer? Lands the carry-out that structure is a training-distribution constraint, not decoration.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B04 (plain-vs-XML product description, paid off with a second concrete case)

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes XML tags are just decoration. They're not — they're a constraint the model was trained to expect. So why does wrapping the same text in XML change the answer Claude gives?

beats.narration_text: The words are identical. So the answer should be too. But formatting alone shifts the quality of what comes back — and that's strange, because nothing about the content changed.

shot.new_visual_element: One content block, two differently-shaped outputs, a question mark between them

production_viz.label: Same words, different result — a puzzle
production_viz.mechanic: A single text block labelled 'SAME WORDS' on cream. Two arrows branch from it to two output shapes of visibly different quality (one thin/uneven, one full/even). A crimson question mark hovers between the branches — the beat's only accent.

beats.act: setup — the concrete case / ANCHOR PLANTED
beats.narration_text: Take one product description. Paste it in as plain text, and Claude's summary is generic. Wrap the exact same words in XML tags, and the summary gets sharp — it pulls the right details out. Same content. Different result.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — plain-text block vs. XML-tagged block, generic summary vs. sharp summary

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — one product description, two summaries
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Left: a plain paragraph labelled 'PLAIN TEXT', arrow to a thin generic summary line. Right: the identical words re-set inside visible tag brackets labelled 'XML-TAGGED', arrow to a fuller, sharper summary line. THIS PRODUCT-DESCRIPTION COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B04 in a second, more granular case.

beats.narration_text: Here's why. Claude was trained on huge amounts of consistently tagged, structured text — documents where title, content, and category always sat inside predictable markup. That built a strong expectation for those shapes. Text that matches the shape it learned gets processed more coherently. Text that doesn't, gets processed less well.

shot.new_visual_element: Before/after pane — plain block left, tagged block right, over a training-distribution curve

production_viz.label: Trained on the shape, expecting the shape
production_viz.mechanic: A wide bell-curve-like distribution drawn low across the frame, labelled 'TRAINING DATA SHAPES'. A tagged-markup block sits directly under the peak (in crimson) with a short 'processed coherently' label; a plain-text block sits out on the low tail (in ink, no accent) with a 'processed less well' label.

beats.narration_text: Look at the difference directly. Plain text: Product Name, Robot Building Kit, two hundred pieces. Tagged: title, content, and category, each wrapped in its own field. Same words. But the tagged version tells Claude exactly where the title ends and the description begins — because that's the shape it was trained to expect.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR PAYOFF — Robot Building Kit, plain sentence vs. tagged fields, side by side

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — Robot Building Kit, field by field
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 COMPOSITION RETURNS, same layout: left, the plain sentence 'Product Name: Robot Building Kit. 200 pieces.' in one undivided block. Right, the same words re-set into three bracketed fields — title, content, category — each boundary marked in crimson. The field boundaries are the only new element versus B02.

beats.narration_text: Wrapping text in XML isn't a trick — it's speaking the shape Claude was trained to expect. Same words, matched structure, a sharper answer.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Open a Claude conversation. Paste in any short paragraph of product or document text, once as plain text, and ask for a summary. Then paste the identical text again, wrapped in XML tags — title, content, category, whatever fields fit — and ask for the same summary. Compare the two answers. Liam, in for Bear.
